home.how.title: How It Works
home.how.sub: Three steps, under a minute — whether it's two friends or a whole bar.
home.step1.title: Start a Room
home.step1.desc: One tap gets you a room code and QR — no accounts, no downloads, no sign-ups. Add the first song yourself or share the code around. And if you step away mid-night, your room and its queue are right where you left them.
home.step2.title: Everyone Adds Songs
home.step2.desc: Anyone in the room scans the code and searches YouTube from their own phone, dropping songs into the shared queue. Karaoke mode finds the best versions automatically.
home.step3.title: Sing on Any Screen
home.step3.desc: Open the display on whatever everyone's facing — TV, laptop, projector, tablet. Lyrics light up as you sing, the host steers the queue, and a QR code lets latecomers jump in.
home.setup.title: What You Need to Host
home.setup.sub: Less than you think — a screen with a browser and something that makes sound. Three ways people run it:
home.setup.card1.title: Just a Laptop or iPad
home.setup.card1.desc: Open KaraoQ, turn up the volume, and you're hosting. The video plays right on the device while everyone queues songs from their phones. Plug in a Bluetooth speaker if the room gets loud.
home.setup.card1.gear1: A laptop, iPad, or any device with a browser
home.setup.card2.title: The Living Room TV
home.setup.card2.desc: Put the song on the big screen — cast with AirPlay or Google Cast, or plug your laptop into the TV with HDMI. The TV's speakers carry the sound, and your device stays the control booth.
home.setup.card3.title: Screen + Sound System
home.setup.card3.desc: Run a laptop into the venue's display and sound system — HDMI to the screen, aux to the speakers. Guests add songs from their phones all night, and mics go through the PA like any other karaoke night.
home.setup.note.strong: No karaoke machine, no microphones required.
home.setup.note.rest: KaraoQ puts the song and lyrics on screen; sound comes from whatever's playing the video. Most living rooms just sing out loud — and if you have mics, run them through your speakers and you're a full venue.

home.faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
home.faq.sub: Everything you need to know before your first song.
home.cta.title: Ready to Sing?
home.cta.sub: Start a karaoke session in seconds. No sign-up required.
faq.free.a: Yes. KaraoQ is free to host and free to join. Songs play from YouTube, so there is nothing to buy or rent.
faq.app.q: Do I need to download an app?
faq.app.a: No downloads and no installs. KaraoQ runs entirely in your web browser on phones, tablets, laptops, and smart TVs.
faq.equipment.q: What equipment do I need to host karaoke night?
faq.equipment.a: A device with a browser and something that makes sound — a laptop or iPad on its own is enough. For a bigger night, put the video on a TV by casting or plugging in with HDMI. No karaoke machine or microphones required.
faq.mics.q: Do I need a microphone for karaoke?
faq.mics.a: No. KaraoQ puts the song and the lyrics on screen, and plenty of living rooms just sing along out loud. A microphone is the upgrade that makes it feel like a real karaoke night — a cheap wireless pair plugged into a Bluetooth speaker's mic input is the setup most people land on. Run the mic through the speaker rather than pairing it to the TV, so voices and backing track come out of the same box and stay in sync.
faq.tv.q: How do I get the karaoke video on my TV?
faq.tv.a: Cast your screen with AirPlay or Google Cast, or connect your laptop to the TV with an HDMI cable. KaraoQ can also pop the video out into its own window, so the TV shows the song and lyrics while the controls stay on your screen.
faq.account.q: Do my guests need an account to sing?
faq.account.a: No sign-up is required for anyone. Guests scan a QR code or enter the room code, then start adding songs from their own phones.
faq.join.q: How do guests join the karaoke session?
faq.join.a: Create a room to get a short join code and QR code. Share either one, and guests can search YouTube and queue songs from their phones in seconds.
faq.songs.q: Where do the karaoke songs come from?
faq.songs.a: Every song streams from YouTube, so you have millions of karaoke tracks, lyric videos, and instrumentals to choose from — no separate karaoke library needed.
faq.venue.q: Can I use KaraoQ at a bar, party, or venue?
faq.venue.a: Absolutely. Cast the queue to any screen and let guests add songs from their phones. It works just as well for house parties, team events, and venue karaoke nights.

guide.athome.title: How to Host Karaoke at Home Without a Machine (Step by Step) | KaraoQ
guide.athome.metaDesc: How to do karaoke at home with no machine: set up the room, get YouTube karaoke on your TV, let guests queue songs from their phones, and keep the night flowing. Free, no downloads, works on any TV.
guide.athome.h1: How to host karaoke at home
guide.athome.intro: You don't need a karaoke machine, a subscription, or a stack of discs to throw a great karaoke night at home. With KaraoQ, any laptop, tablet, or phone becomes the whole setup: you search YouTube for the songs everyone already loves, guests add them to a shared queue from their own phones, and the lyrics play on whatever screen you have. Here's how to set it up in a couple of minutes — and the small things that make the difference between a quiet room and one that won't stop.
guide.athome.sec1.title: Set up the room before anyone arrives
guide.athome.sec1.body:
Put the lyrics on the biggest screen in the room and face the seating toward it — people sing along when they can read the words from the couch. If you have any speaker with an aux input, plug it into the laptop's headphone jack rather than relying on the TV's speakers; it's louder, fuller, and it keeps the music in time with the words. Leave a clear spot in front of the screen for the singer. That's the stage.

Dim the main lights and leave a lamp on. It sounds trivial and it's the single biggest lever for getting shy people to sing — nobody wants a spotlight in a bright kitchen.
guide.athome.sec2.title: Do you need a microphone?
guide.athome.sec2.body:
For eight people in a living room, honestly no — a first night with no mic works fine and costs nothing. A mic changes the feel from 'singing along' to 'performing', which is what you want once people are into it. The cheapest good option is a wireless karaoke mic with its own built-in speaker; the best value for a real party is a Bluetooth party speaker with a mic input and a wired mic plugged into it.

Whatever you choose, the microphone goes into a speaker, never into the TV or the phone — that's the one rule that keeps the singer's voice in sync with the music. The gear guides below cover the rest.
guide.athome.sec3.title: Running the night so it never stalls
guide.athome.sec3.body:
Seed the queue with three or four crowd songs before guests arrive so there's never a silence while people decide. Sing the first one yourself, badly — it sets the bar at exactly the right height. Encourage duets and group songs early; a nervous singer will join a chorus long before they'll take a verse alone.

Keep the queue fair. Because everyone adds from their own phone, the order takes care of itself, and the screen shows who's up next so people can get a drink and be back in time. If a song is dragging, skip it from your phone — nobody has to walk up to the screen.
guide.athome.step1.title: Open a room on any device
guide.athome.step1.body: Go to KaraoQ in your browser and create a room. There's nothing to download and no account to make — you get a short join code and a QR code straight away.
guide.athome.step2.title: Share the code so guests can join
guide.athome.step2.body: Show the QR code or read out the room code. Guests scan or type it on their own phones and they're in — no app, no sign-up, and nothing to set up on their end.
guide.athome.step3.title: Build the queue from everyone's phones
guide.athome.step3.body: Everyone searches YouTube from their phone and adds songs to one shared queue. KaraoQ plays them in order, so there's no fighting over the laptop and no one hogs the mic.
guide.athome.step4.title: Put the words on the biggest screen
guide.athome.step4.body: Open KaraoQ's display in your smart TV's browser, cast it with AirPlay or Google Cast, or plug in with an HDMI cable. The TV shows the song and lyrics while you keep the controls on your phone.
guide.athome.faq1.q: How do I do karaoke at home without a machine?
guide.athome.faq1.a: Open KaraoQ in a browser, create a room, and put the display on your TV — via the TV's own browser, casting, or an HDMI cable from a laptop. Songs come from YouTube, guests queue from their phones, and the lyrics show on the screen. A karaoke machine's only remaining job, the speaker and mic, is optional.
guide.athome.faq2.q: How many people does it work for?
guide.athome.faq2.a: From two to a full house. Everyone joins from their own phone with the room code, and the shared queue keeps turns in order however many people add to it. For more than about fifteen, a speaker with a mic input becomes worth it so the singer can be heard.
guide.athome.faq3.a: Very well — kids love queuing their own songs from a phone or tablet. Search results come from YouTube's karaoke channels, and the host can remove anything from the queue on their phone. A pair of wireless karaoke mics with built-in speakers is the classic kids' addition.
guide.athome.faq4.a: Nothing. KaraoQ is free to host and free to join, there's no app to buy and no account to make, and the songs play from YouTube. If you later want a speaker and mics, the cheap setup guide below shows what's worth buying and what isn't.
guide.athome.closing: That's it — no machine, no library, no clutter. As long as one device has a browser and something that makes sound, you can host karaoke anywhere: a living room, a dorm, a backyard, or a hotel room on a trip.
guide.tv.title: How to Do Karaoke on Your TV (Any Smart TV, Fire Stick, Roku, HDMI) | KaraoQ
guide.tv.metaDesc: Get YouTube karaoke lyrics on your TV without a machine. Step-by-step for Samsung and LG smart TVs, Chromecast, Apple TV, Fire TV Stick, Roku and plain HDMI — plus the fix for the mic delay everyone hits.
guide.tv.h1: How to do karaoke on your TV
guide.tv.intro: A TV turns a phone-sized karaoke session into a proper show — big lyrics everyone can read from the couch. You don't need a karaoke machine or a TV karaoke subscription to get there. KaraoQ runs in a browser, so the words can reach your screen five different ways: the TV's own browser, casting, AirPlay, a streaming stick, or a cable. Below is the fastest path for every kind of TV, and the one audio setting that stops your voice from arriving a beat late.
guide.tv.sec1.title: The no-gadget way: open KaraoQ in the TV's browser
guide.tv.sec1.body:
If your TV has a web browser — most Samsung and LG sets do, and Fire TV has Silk — you don't need to cast anything. Create a room on your phone, then on the TV open the browser and go to the display address shown on your host screen (it ends in your room code). Tap once on the remote to allow playback and the TV becomes the karaoke screen: current song, lyrics, and who's up next. Your phone stays the remote, and guests queue from theirs.

This works well on TVs from about 2020 onwards. Older sets run very old browsers and may refuse to play video; if that happens, use one of the routes below instead. The TV browser also fixes the delay problem by design — the music comes out of the TV, and there's nothing wireless in the chain to lag.
guide.tv.sec2.title: Chromecast and Google TV
guide.tv.sec2.body:
On a laptop, open KaraoQ's display view in Chrome, click the three-dot menu, choose Cast, and pick your TV — this casts just that tab. From an Android phone, use screen mirroring from the Google Home app or your phone's Cast tile. Both send video and audio together, so the words and the music stay in sync on the TV.

Tab casting re-encodes the picture, so on a busy Wi-Fi network it can stutter. If it does, drop the casting quality to 480p (the lyrics are still perfectly readable) or move the router closer. A Google TV device can also install a browser, at which point the no-gadget route above applies.
guide.tv.sec3.title: Apple TV and AirPlay
guide.tv.sec3.body:
From an iPhone, iPad or Mac, open Control Center, choose Screen Mirroring and pick your Apple TV — or any recent Samsung, LG or Roku TV, since most of them now accept AirPlay directly. Open KaraoQ's display view and it fills the TV.

Mirroring carries the audio with the picture, so lyrics and music stay locked together. If the room's speaker seems slightly behind, Apple TV has a fix under Settings → Video and Audio → Wireless Audio Sync. Note that Apple's own TV karaoke needs an Apple Music subscription; the YouTube route through AirPlay is free.
guide.tv.sec4.title: Amazon Fire TV Stick
guide.tv.sec4.body:
Every Fire TV Stick ships with the Silk browser, so the easiest path is to open KaraoQ's display address directly on the stick — no phone mirroring needed. Use the remote to type the address once; the TV then runs the show on its own.

Android phones can also mirror to a Fire Stick through the Display Mirroring setting. iPhones can't AirPlay to a Fire Stick without a third-party receiver app, so if your household is iPhone-only, the Silk browser or an HDMI cable is the cleaner choice.
guide.tv.sec5.title: Roku
guide.tv.sec5.body:
Roku is the one platform with no real web browser, so you have to send the picture to it. Newer 4K Roku players and Roku TVs accept AirPlay from iPhones and Macs; Windows laptops and most Android phones can screen-mirror to any Roku. Open KaraoQ's display view on the sending device and it appears on the TV.

Mirroring to a Roku adds a small delay, but because the sound travels with the picture it stays in sync with the lyrics. For a permanent living-room setup, an HDMI cable from a laptop is the more reliable option.
guide.tv.sec6.title: The reliable way: an HDMI cable
guide.tv.sec6.body:
Plug a laptop into the TV with an HDMI cable, choose the TV as a second screen, and drag KaraoQ's display window onto it. There's no Wi-Fi to blame, zero lag, and it works on any TV made in the last twenty years. Phones work too: a USB-C to HDMI adapter for Android and recent iPhones, or Apple's Lightning AV adapter for older iPhones.

This is the setup most regular hosts end up with, because the laptop also gives you a place to plug in a speaker and mics — which is where the next section comes in.
guide.tv.sec7.title: Fix the delay: get the sound out of the TV
guide.tv.sec7.body:
The most common complaint with TV karaoke is hearing your own voice a fraction of a second late. It almost never comes from the app — it comes from the sound chain. A TV takes a moment to process audio; a soundbar on optical or HDMI ARC adds more; a Bluetooth speaker or Bluetooth microphone adds a clearly audible gap on top.

The fix is to keep the singer's voice out of the TV entirely. Run the microphone into a speaker (a party speaker with a mic input, or a mic with its own built-in speaker) and, if you can, feed the music into that same speaker from the laptop's headphone jack instead of through the TV. Voice and backing track then come out of one box, in sync, and the TV only has to show the words. If you'd rather keep the TV speakers, switch the picture to Game mode and turn off any AV sync or audio delay setting — Samsung calls it Digital Output Audio Delay, LG calls it AV Sync Adjustment.
guide.tv.step1.title: Create the room and note the display address
guide.tv.step1.body: Open KaraoQ in your browser and create a room. The host screen shows a short join code for guests and a display address for the TV — that address is all any screen needs.
guide.tv.step2.title: Get the display onto the TV
guide.tv.step2.body: Pick the route for your TV from the list above: type the display address into the TV's browser, cast or mirror it from a phone or laptop, or plug in over HDMI. Tap once to allow playback if the TV asks.
guide.tv.step3.title: Keep the controls on your phone
guide.tv.step3.body: The TV only ever shows the song, the lyrics and who's up next. Skipping, reordering and pausing stay on your phone or laptop, so nobody walks up to the screen mid-chorus.
guide.tv.step4.title: Let guests queue from their seats
guide.tv.step4.body: Guests scan the QR code on the TV, search YouTube on their own phones and add songs to the shared queue. The lineup builds itself while the current singer has the screen.
guide.tv.faq1.q: Can I do karaoke on a smart TV without a karaoke machine?
guide.tv.faq1.a: Yes. Any TV that can show a web page or receive a cast can be the lyrics screen. KaraoQ plays karaoke tracks from YouTube in the browser, so the machine's two jobs — song library and lyrics display — are already covered. A microphone and a speaker are all you add, and even those are optional for a first night.
guide.tv.faq2.q: Does it work on a Samsung or LG TV?
guide.tv.faq2.a: Yes. Both have a built-in browser: open it and go to your room's display address. Sets from roughly 2020 onwards handle it well; older ones may struggle to play video, in which case AirPlay (both brands support it on recent models) or an HDMI cable does the job. Samsung's own karaoke app on 2025 TVs needs a subscription — this route is free.
guide.tv.faq3.q: How do I do karaoke on a Roku or Fire Stick?
guide.tv.faq3.a: Fire TV Stick: open the Silk browser and type in the display address — that's it. Roku has no browser, so mirror from a phone or laptop instead: AirPlay works on 4K Rokus and Roku TVs, and Windows or Android can screen-mirror to any Roku. On either device, an HDMI cable from a laptop is the fallback that always works.
guide.tv.faq4.q: Why is my voice delayed when I sing through the TV?
guide.tv.faq4.a: Because the sound is taking the slow road: TV processing, then a soundbar over optical or ARC, then possibly Bluetooth. Each hop adds a few dozen milliseconds and your ear notices the total. Route the mic into a speaker instead of the TV, and ideally send the music to that same speaker too. If you must use TV audio, use Game picture mode and switch off audio delay settings.
guide.tv.faq5.q: Casting or HDMI — which is better for karaoke?
guide.tv.faq5.a: HDMI, if a laptop can sit near the TV: zero lag, no Wi-Fi dependence, and a headphone jack to feed a speaker. Casting is fine for a casual night and needs no cables — video and audio arrive together so the lyrics stay in time — but it can stutter on crowded Wi-Fi and pairs badly with a separate speaker. The TV's own browser beats both when it's available.
guide.tv.closing: Whichever route fits your TV, the screen only ever shows the song and the words — the controls stay private on your phone, and guests never have to touch the TV. Keep the singer's voice out of the TV's audio chain and karaoke on the big screen needs no dedicated hardware at all.
guide.youtube.title: Free YouTube Karaoke: How to Sing With YouTube at Home (No Downloads) | KaraoQ
guide.youtube.metaDesc: Turn YouTube into a free karaoke library. How to find the right karaoke version, what to do when a song has none, how to handle ads and unplayable videos, and how to build a shared queue from everyone's phones — no subscription, no downloads.
guide.youtube.h1: Free YouTube karaoke for any party
guide.youtube.intro: YouTube is the biggest karaoke library in the world — millions of instrumentals, lyric videos, and karaoke tracks, all free. The trouble with running a party straight off YouTube is everything around the songs: hunting for a good version, passing the laptop around, ads landing mid-chorus. KaraoQ turns that library into a real karaoke night: searchable, queued, and shared across everyone's phones, with the lyrics on any screen. Here's how to get the most out of it.
guide.youtube.sec1.title: How to find the right karaoke version
guide.youtube.sec1.body:
Search the song title in KaraoQ and the results come from YouTube's karaoke channels first — Sing King, KaraFun, Stingray, Party Tyme and the like — so you rarely have to type the word 'karaoke' yourself. When several versions come up, pick the one with scrolling on-screen lyrics from a channel you recognise; the big channels re-record the backing track faithfully and time the words properly.

For a nervous singer or a big ballad, look for a piano or acoustic karaoke version — a solo piano is far more forgiving than a full arrangement. For songs the whole room half-knows, a lyric video of the original works surprisingly well too.
guide.youtube.sec2.title: When a song has no karaoke version
guide.youtube.sec2.body:
Search the song plus 'instrumental' — producers upload official instrumentals for a surprising number of tracks, and smaller karaoke channels cover an astonishing long tail. Failing that, a lyric video of the original lets everyone sing over the record, which for a group singalong is often more fun than a sterile backing track anyway.

If you have the original file and a laptop, free AI vocal-removal tools can strip the vocals from a track in a minute or two, and several karaoke channels take requests. But for a party, the fastest fix is the honest one: if a song isn't there, the next one in the queue is.
guide.youtube.sec3.title: Ads, and the other things that interrupt
guide.youtube.sec3.body:
Songs play from YouTube, so YouTube's ads can play too. A YouTube Premium account on the device that runs the display removes them completely — worth it for a night with twenty songs — and since the display is one device, one account covers the whole party.

Occasionally an uploader has disabled playback outside YouTube, and the video won't start on any website. KaraoQ tells the room straight away so you can pick another version — usually the same song from a different channel is one tap away. Keep the queue a few songs deep and no single video can stall the night.
guide.youtube.step1.title: Search the songs everyone knows
guide.youtube.step1.body: Type any song into KaraoQ and it searches YouTube for the best karaoke and lyric versions. From throwback pop to the latest hits in any language, if it's on YouTube, it's ready to sing.
guide.youtube.step2.title: Add to one shared queue
guide.youtube.step2.body: Every guest adds songs from their own phone to a single shared queue. KaraoQ plays them back to back in order, so the night flows without anyone touching the laptop.
guide.youtube.step3.title: Sing along to the words on screen
guide.youtube.step3.body: The song streams straight from YouTube with the lyrics right there on screen — on a phone, a laptop, or the TV. Nothing to install and nothing to rip or download.
guide.youtube.step4.title: Keep it free from start to finish
guide.youtube.step4.body: KaraoQ is free to host and free to join, and the songs are free because they play from YouTube. There's nothing to buy, rent, or subscribe to — just open a room and start singing.
guide.youtube.faq1.a: Yes. Karaoke channels publish their tracks free on YouTube, and KaraoQ plays them straight from YouTube at no cost — free to host, free to join, no subscription. You'll see YouTube's usual ads unless the display device has YouTube Premium.
guide.youtube.faq2.q: Can I do karaoke with YouTube on my TV?
guide.youtube.faq2.a: Yes. Open KaraoQ's display in your smart TV's browser, cast it from a phone or laptop, or connect a laptop with an HDMI cable. The TV shows the song and lyrics while everyone queues from their phones. The TV guide below walks through every kind of TV and streaming stick.
guide.youtube.faq3.q: How do I stop passing the laptop around?
guide.youtube.faq3.a: That's the whole point of KaraoQ. Create a room, show the QR code, and everyone searches YouTube and adds songs from their own phone into one shared queue. The host's controls stay on their phone too, so the laptop just plays.
guide.youtube.faq4.q: Why does a video say it can't be played?
guide.youtube.faq4.a: The uploader has disabled playback on other websites, which blocks it everywhere outside YouTube itself. It's rare on the big karaoke channels. KaraoQ flags it immediately; search the song again and pick a version from another channel.
guide.youtube.faq5.a: No, but it helps. Without it, ads can appear between or before songs. Signing into a Premium account on the single device that runs the display removes them for the whole room, since guests' phones only ever queue — they don't play video.
guide.youtube.closing: Because it's all YouTube, your karaoke library is effectively endless and always up to date with the songs people actually want to sing. Add a shared queue and a screen for the words, and it's the simplest, cheapest way to run karaoke for a party — and it costs nothing.
guide.setups.title: Home Karaoke Setup Guide: 5 Levels From Free to a Full PA (2026) | KaraoQ
guide.setups.metaDesc: The complete home karaoke setup guide, from a $0 phone-and-TV night to a mixer, powered speakers and wireless mics. What each level costs, what to buy, what to skip, and how to wire it — with the song library free from YouTube.
guide.setups.h1: Home karaoke setup: five levels, from free to a full PA
guide.setups.intro: Every karaoke machine ever sold is the same three things in one box: microphone inputs, a small mixer for volume and echo, and an amplified speaker. The fourth thing — the songs and the lyrics screen — used to be the expensive part, and it's now free: KaraoQ plays millions of karaoke tracks from YouTube in any browser, with a shared queue everyone fills from their phones. That leaves you free to spend as much or as little on sound as you like. Here are the five levels people actually land on, from what you already own to a rig that fills a garage, with the mistakes each level tends to make.
guide.setups.sec1.title: Level 0 — $0: what you already own
guide.setups.sec1.body:
A TV or laptop for the lyrics, the TV's speakers for the music, and no microphone at all. Open KaraoQ, share the room code, and let everyone queue from their phones. It sounds like a compromise and it's genuinely how most people run their first night — a living room of eight people singing along doesn't need amplification.

What goes wrong: TV speakers are thin on vocals, and if the music is going out to a Bluetooth speaker from the TV it will drift behind the lyrics. If you own any speaker with an aux input, plug it into the laptop's headphone jack instead of the TV and both problems disappear. Spend nothing until you know you'll do this again.
guide.setups.sec2.title: Level 1 — under $50: the all-in-one Bluetooth mic
guide.setups.sec2.body:
The handheld karaoke microphone with a speaker built into the grip. Your phone streams the music to the mic over Bluetooth, your voice goes into the same little speaker, and both come out together — which is exactly why it works despite being a toy: your voice never crosses Bluetooth, so there's no delay to hear. Kids adore them, and a two-pack covers duets.

What goes wrong: people expect to pair one to the TV as a microphone. It can't — it's a Bluetooth receiver, not a transmitter — and a TV wouldn't accept a mic that way anyway. Play the music from your phone into the mic, or just use the mic's own speaker for voice while the TV carries the track. The other limit is volume: it won't carry over a loud party, which is what the next level fixes.
guide.setups.sec3.title: Level 2 — $100 to $200: a party speaker with a mic input
guide.setups.sec3.body:
This is the sweet spot for most homes and the setup that quietly replaced the karaoke machine. Buy a Bluetooth party speaker that has a quarter-inch microphone jack (ideally two) and an echo knob, plug in a wired mic, and send the music from your laptop or phone. Voice and backing track come out of one box, in sync, loud enough for a backyard, and the same speaker does duty for every other party. Battery models go wherever the crowd goes. The plug-and-play version of this level is a portable Bluetooth PA that ships with two wireless mics in the box — around $200 and nothing to think about.

What goes wrong: sending the music over Bluetooth while the lyrics play on the TV. The speaker will be a beat behind the words. Use the aux cable from the laptop's headphone jack — the lyrics and the music then leave the same device at the same moment. Also check the cable that comes with a cheap mic: a quarter-inch plug with two black rings is a stereo plug and gives silence in a mono mic jack; you want one ring.
guide.setups.sec4.title: Level 3 — $300 to $600: mixer, powered speaker, proper mics
guide.setups.sec4.body:
The setup every enthusiast forum converges on, and the one karaoke bars quietly run. A small analog mixer with built-in effects (an 8- or 12-channel model with reverb is plenty; a USB model also lets you record the night), one or two powered PA speakers, and dynamic handheld microphones — the SM58, which regulars call the gold standard for a reason, or its famously good budget clone at a fifth of the price. The laptop plugs into a stereo line channel on the mixer, each mic gets its own channel with its own volume and echo, and the mixer feeds the speaker. An HDMI cable takes the lyrics to the TV.

Why this beats a $500 karaoke machine: every part is repairable, replaceable and useful for something else, and powered PA speakers are built to take a dropped mic and a screaming chorus where home hi-fi speakers, soundbars and little Bluetooth speakers are not. What goes wrong: buying a condenser microphone because it looked professional — it hears the backing track as much as the singer — or a bargain VHF wireless set, which has terrible dynamic range. Stick to wired dynamic cardioid mics for live singing.
guide.setups.sec5.title: Level 4 — $600 and up: wireless mics and a second speaker
guide.setups.sec5.body:
Once the room is bigger than a living room, cables become the problem. A dual-channel UHF wireless microphone system (avoid 2.4 GHz sets, which share the airwaves with your Wi-Fi and drop out at the worst moment) frees two singers to roam. A second powered speaker gives you stereo and lets you angle one back toward the singers as a monitor so they can hear themselves — the single biggest reason people sing better at a bar than at home. Premium all-in-one PA speakers with a three-channel mixer built in collapse the mixer and speaker into one carryable box if you'd rather not run cables at all.

What goes wrong: feedback. Keep speakers in front of the singer pointing at the audience, keep the mic close to the mouth and never cupped around the head, and bring the mic volume up until it just rings, then back off a touch.
guide.setups.sec6.title: Sound better through any of it: reverb, mic technique, headroom
guide.setups.sec6.body:
Three habits from people who run karaoke every week. First, add a little reverb on the mic channel — not for the audience, for the singer. A dry voice in a living room sounds thin and makes people push too hard; a touch of reverb lets them hear themselves and settle their volume. Second, hold the mic vertically with the ball just under the chin and sing across the top of it, and turn the bass down on the mic channel. Both fight the boominess you get from a mic held close.

Third, leave headroom. Set the mic level so a loud chorus doesn't clip, and if your mixer has a one-knob compressor on the mic channels, turn it up a little so the loudest notes get tamed instead of distorting. And whatever you do, don't run vocals through a soundbar or a small Bluetooth speaker — they handle the music fine but were never built for the peaks a voice produces, and they distort or die.
guide.setups.sec7.title: The part every level shares: the screen and the songs
guide.setups.sec7.body: Whatever you spend on sound, the lyrics screen and the song library stay the same, and stay free. Get KaraoQ's display onto the TV — its own browser, casting, or HDMI from the laptop — and keep the host controls on your phone. Guests join by QR code, search YouTube from their own phones and add to one shared queue, so nobody has to run the laptop or pass a binder around. The night runs itself while you're plugging in the second mic.
guide.setups.step1.title: Get the music out of the laptop, not the TV
guide.setups.step1.body: Run a 3.5 mm cable from the laptop's headphone jack to the speaker's aux input, or to a stereo line channel on the mixer. The TV then only shows the picture, which removes the delay a TV's audio processing adds.
guide.setups.step2.title: Plug the mics into the speaker or mixer
guide.setups.step2.body: Microphones go into the mic jacks, never into the TV or the phone. Give each singer their own channel if the mixer has them, and set a touch of reverb — it flatters every voice.
guide.setups.step3.title: Put the lyrics on the TV
guide.setups.step3.body: HDMI from the laptop to the TV is the zero-lag option. Open KaraoQ's display view on that screen; the host controls stay on your phone. On a smart TV, you can skip the cable and open the display address in the TV's browser.
guide.setups.step4.title: Sound-check before the first guest
guide.setups.step4.body: Play a song, speak into each mic, and set music and voice so the voice sits just on top. Raise the mic until it rings, then back off. Two minutes now saves the first three songs of the night.
guide.setups.itemsHeading: What to buy, level by level
guide.setups.itemsIntro: Search links rather than specific models, so they stay current — the copy tells you what to look for in each category. Roughly in the order you'd buy them.
guide.setups.item1.name: Bluetooth karaoke microphone with built-in speaker
guide.setups.item1.body: Level 1. Look for a two-pack, a decent battery rating, and USB-C charging. Don't expect party volume; do expect kids to fight over it.
guide.setups.item2.name: Bluetooth party speaker with microphone input
guide.setups.item2.body: Level 2, and the single best purchase in this guide. Insist on a quarter-inch mic jack (two is better), an echo control, and an aux input so the music can come in by cable rather than Bluetooth.
guide.setups.item3.name: Wired dynamic vocal microphone (XLR)
guide.setups.item3.body: Levels 2 to 4. A dynamic cardioid handheld — the SM58 or its budget clones. Nearly indestructible, rejects the backing track, and needs no batteries. Buy two.
guide.setups.item4.name: Small analog mixer with effects
guide.setups.item4.body: Level 3. An 8- to 12-channel mixer with built-in reverb: XLR channels for the mics, a stereo line channel for the laptop, one main output to the speaker. Per-singer volume and echo is what makes it feel like a karaoke bar.
guide.setups.item5.name: Powered PA speaker (12-inch)
guide.setups.item5.body: Levels 3 and 4. Powered means the amplifier is inside; 12-inch is the size that fills a house without needing a subwoofer. Many have a mic input built in, so you can start with the speaker alone and add the mixer later.
guide.setups.item6.name: Dual UHF wireless microphone system
guide.setups.item6.body: Level 4. Two handhelds and one receiver that plugs into the mixer. UHF, not 2.4 GHz — the latter shares spectrum with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and cuts out in a house full of phones.
guide.setups.item7.name: 3.5 mm to dual 1/4-inch cable
guide.setups.item7.body: Every level from 2 up. This is the cable that carries the music from the laptop's headphone jack into the speaker or mixer, and it's the one nobody remembers to buy. A 3.5 mm to RCA version does the same job on speakers with RCA inputs.
guide.setups.item8.name: XLR microphone cables and a mic stand
guide.setups.item8.body: Levels 3 and 4. One XLR cable per wired mic (25 feet is the useful length) and a stand so the mic has somewhere to live between singers. Cheap, and the difference between a rig and a pile of gear.
guide.setups.faq1.q: Do I need a karaoke machine for home karaoke?
guide.setups.faq1.a: No. A karaoke machine bundles mic inputs, a small mixer and a speaker with a song catalog, and the catalog was the part that justified the price. YouTube made it free, and KaraoQ turns it into a shared, queued karaoke night. A party speaker with a mic input does the machine's remaining job better, and for less.
guide.setups.faq2.q: Do I need a mixer for home karaoke?
guide.setups.faq2.a: Not until Level 3. A party speaker with a mic jack has a tiny mixer built in — that's what the echo and mic volume knobs are. A separate mixer earns its place when you want two or more singers on their own channels, real reverb, and a speaker that isn't tied to one brand's features.
guide.setups.faq3.q: Karaoke machine or Bluetooth speaker with a mic — which should I buy?
guide.setups.faq3.a: The speaker, almost always. A karaoke-branded machine is often flimsier and pricier than an equivalent party speaker, and its built-in song library is the one part you don't need. The exception is a young child's first setup, where the lights and the cheap disc player are the point.
guide.setups.faq4.q: Why is my voice delayed through the microphone?
guide.setups.faq4.a: Because it's travelling through something slow: Bluetooth adds a clearly audible gap, and a TV or soundbar adds more while it processes audio. Plug the mic into a speaker or mixer, not the TV or the phone, and send the music into that same speaker by cable from the laptop. If voice and track come out of one box, there's nothing left to lag.
guide.setups.faq5.a: Wired for value and reliability: no batteries, no dropouts, and a great dynamic mic costs less than a bad wireless one. Go wireless when the room is big enough that cables are a trip hazard, and then buy a UHF system — 2.4 GHz mics fight with your Wi-Fi.
guide.setups.faq6.q: What's the best home karaoke setup for the money?
guide.setups.faq6.a: For most homes, Level 2: a party speaker with a mic input, a wired dynamic mic or two, and an aux cable from the laptop, with the lyrics on the TV over HDMI or the TV's browser. It's a couple of hundred dollars, it works for every other party too, and the software side — songs, queue, lyrics — costs nothing with KaraoQ.
guide.setups.closing: Start at whichever level matches the next party, not the imagined one. The nice thing about building it in parts is that nothing is wasted: the wired mic from Level 2 plugs into the Level 3 mixer, the mixer feeds the Level 4 wireless receiver, and the screen and the songs stay free at every step.
guide.venue.title: Karaoke for Bars & Venues — Guests Queue From Their Phones | KaraoQ
guide.venue.metaDesc: Run karaoke at your bar or venue without a KJ or a dedicated machine. Guests scan a QR code, queue songs from their phones, and sing to any screen. Free to run, nothing to install.
guide.venue.h1: Karaoke for bars, parties and venues
guide.venue.intro: Running karaoke at a bar, party, or event usually means a host, a laptop full of files, and a line of people waiting to hand over a slip of paper. KaraoQ replaces all of it: guests queue their own songs from their phones, the lineup manages itself, and the words play on any screen you already have. Here's how to run a karaoke night that scales to a full room.
guide.venue.step1.title: Put a QR code on the tables
guide.venue.step1.body: Create a room and print or display the QR code and join code. Guests scan it from anywhere in the room and join instantly — no app to download and no account to create.
guide.venue.step2.title: Let guests queue their own songs
guide.venue.step2.body: Everyone searches YouTube and adds songs from their own phone. The shared queue keeps every turn in order, so staff never have to run a paper list or babysit a laptop.
guide.venue.step3.title: Show the lineup on your screens
guide.venue.step3.body: Cast or plug KaraoQ into the venue's TV or projector. The screen shows the current singer, the lyrics, and who's up next, so the whole room can follow along.
guide.venue.step4.title: Keep the energy up with reactions
guide.venue.step4.body: Guests cheer and react from their phones, and reactions light up the screen in real time. It turns a quiet open mic into a room that's actually into it — with no extra staff.
guide.venue.closing: KaraoQ is free to run and needs no dedicated karaoke machine, so it works just as well for a weekly bar night, a private party, or a one-off event. Set up a room, share the code, and let the room run its own karaoke.
guide.gear.title: Cheap Home Karaoke Setup (Under $200): What You Actually Need | KaraoQ
guide.gear.metaDesc: Build a home karaoke setup for under $200. The songs and lyrics screen are free with KaraoQ and YouTube, so your money goes to one speaker and a mic. The short shopping list, the Bluetooth delay trap to avoid, and why a party speaker beats a karaoke machine.
guide.gear.h1: The cheap home karaoke setup that actually works
guide.gear.intro: The secret to cheap home karaoke is that the expensive part — the songs and the machine — is now free. KaraoQ plays millions of karaoke tracks straight from YouTube in your browser, with a shared queue everyone fills from their phones, so the whole software side costs nothing. That leaves the physical bits: something to hear the music on, something to sing into, and a screen for the lyrics. You probably own half of it already. Here's what's worth buying for under $200, the one mistake that ruins most first attempts, and what you can skip entirely.
guide.gear.sec1.title: Why a karaoke machine is the wrong thing to buy
guide.gear.sec1.body:
Open up any home karaoke machine and you'll find a speaker, a couple of microphone jacks, a volume-and-echo circuit, and a way to play songs. The song part is what you were paying for, and it's the part that dates fastest — a disc slot, a bundled catalog, an app that stops being updated. YouTube plus KaraoQ replaces it for free and never runs out of songs.

What's left is a speaker with mic jacks, and the party speaker aisle does that better: louder, sturdier, battery-powered, and useful for every other gathering. Karaoke-branded machines in the same price range are routinely flimsier than the equivalent party speaker. Unless you're buying for a small child who wants the lights and the disc slot, buy the speaker.
guide.gear.sec2.title: The Bluetooth delay trap
guide.gear.sec2.body:
Almost every disappointing home karaoke setup has the same cause: the singer's voice arrives a fraction of a second after they sing, and it's impossible to stay in time. Bluetooth is the usual culprit — it adds a delay you can clearly hear — and a TV or soundbar adds more while it processes the audio. A microphone paired to a TV, or music going from the TV out to a Bluetooth speaker, both fall into this trap.

The rule that avoids it: the microphone goes into the speaker, never into the TV or the phone, and the music comes into that same speaker by cable from the laptop's headphone jack rather than over Bluetooth. Voice and backing track then leave one box at the same instant, and the TV is only there to show the words. The all-in-one Bluetooth mics with a built-in speaker follow the same rule by accident, which is why they work at all.
guide.gear.sec3.title: Wired mics are the budget move
guide.gear.sec3.body:
Cheap wireless karaoke mics drop out, eat batteries and often pair over 2.4 GHz, where they fight with every phone in the house. A wired dynamic handheld microphone — the type used on every stage in the world — costs less than a mediocre wireless one, needs no batteries, rejects the backing track, and survives being dropped. Buy two for duets, plus a cable each.

One detail that catches people: a quarter-inch plug with two black rings is a stereo plug and gives silence in a mono mic jack. You want the one-ring version, or an XLR cable if your speaker has an XLR input.
guide.gear.step1.title: Start with what's free: the screen and the songs
guide.gear.step1.body: Open KaraoQ in a browser and you have the song library, the shared queue, and the lyrics display handled. Any TV, laptop, tablet, or even a phone propped on the coffee table works as the lyrics screen — spend nothing here until you know you need more.
guide.gear.step2.title: Buy one speaker with a microphone input
guide.gear.step2.body: A Bluetooth party speaker with a quarter-inch mic jack and an echo knob is the whole PA. Feed it the music by aux cable from the laptop, not over Bluetooth, so the sound stays in step with the lyrics on the TV. Battery models follow the party outside.
guide.gear.step3.title: Add microphones — into the speaker, not the TV
guide.gear.step3.body: A pair of wired dynamic mics is the best value; a two-pack of wireless karaoke mics with their own built-in speakers is the zero-setup alternative. Either way the voice goes into a speaker, never into the TV, so it stays in sync with the music.
guide.gear.step4.title: Get the lyrics on the big screen
guide.gear.step4.body: Open KaraoQ's display in your smart TV's browser, cast it from a laptop or phone, or plug the laptop in over HDMI. The cable is the zero-lag, zero-fuss option and puts the laptop's headphone jack right next to the speaker. Guests keep queuing songs from their own phones throughout.
guide.gear.itemsIntro: Six things, in order of impact. The first two are the whole setup for most living rooms — the rest is polish. Links are category searches so they never go stale.
guide.gear.item1.name: Bluetooth party speaker with microphone input
guide.gear.item1.body: The heart of the setup and the one thing worth spending on. Insist on a quarter-inch mic jack (two is better), an echo control and an aux input. Pick a battery model if the party ever moves to the garden.
guide.gear.item2.name: Wired dynamic vocal microphones
guide.gear.item2.body: The stage standard and its budget clones. Nearly indestructible, no batteries, and a cardioid pattern that hears the singer rather than the speaker. Two of these plus cables cost less than one flaky wireless set.
guide.gear.item3.name: 3.5 mm to 1/4-inch aux cable
guide.gear.item3.body: Laptop headphone jack to the speaker's aux input. This is what keeps the music in time with the lyrics — and the cable nobody remembers until the party has started. Get the RCA version instead if that's what your speaker has.
guide.gear.item4.name: HDMI cable (10 ft)
guide.gear.item4.body: Laptop to TV, done. No lag, no dropped connection mid-chorus, and it works on any TV. Ten feet reaches from the couch to the screen.
guide.gear.item5.name: Wireless karaoke microphones with built-in speaker (2-pack)
guide.gear.item5.body: The zero-setup option for kids and small rooms: your voice and the music come out of the mic itself, so there's nothing to wire and no delay to hear. Not loud enough for a full party — that's what the speaker above is for.
guide.gear.item6.name: All-in-one karaoke machine (optional)
guide.gear.item6.body: Speaker, mic inputs and lights in one box. Skip it for adults — the party speaker does the same job better — but for a child's first setup the lights and the simplicity are the point.
guide.gear.faq1.q: How much does a home karaoke setup cost?
guide.gear.faq1.a: As little as nothing: KaraoQ and its YouTube song library are free, so a TV and a phone are technically a complete setup. A party speaker with a mic input and a pair of wired mics — the setup most people land on — comes in under $200 in the US, with no subscription on top. Anything beyond that is for bigger rooms.
guide.gear.faq2.q: Do I need a karaoke machine?
guide.gear.faq2.a: No. A karaoke machine bundles a speaker, mic inputs, and a song catalog — but the catalog is the part that used to cost money, and YouTube made it free. A Bluetooth party speaker with a mic input does the same job, and KaraoQ replaces the catalog, the queue, and the lyrics screen.
guide.gear.faq3.a: Not at this budget. The mic volume and echo knobs on a party speaker are a small mixer already. A separate mixer is worth it later, when you want two singers on their own channels and real reverb — that's the next level up, covered in the full setup guide.
guide.gear.faq4.q: What's the cheapest way to get lyrics on the TV?
guide.gear.faq4.a: Your smart TV's own browser, if it has one — open the display address and you're done. Next is an HDMI cable from a laptop, often one you already own, then casting with AirPlay or Google Cast. A streaming stick is only needed for older TVs that can't do any of those.
guide.gear.faq5.q: Why do the vocals lag behind the music on my wireless mic?
guide.gear.faq5.a: That happens when the mic pairs to the TV or phone over Bluetooth — the round-trip adds a delay you can hear. Route the mic into the speaker instead (via its receiver or a cable), or use a mic with its own built-in speaker. Voice and backing track then come out of the same box, in sync.
guide.gear.faq6.a: Wired, on a budget: no batteries, no dropouts, and better sound per dollar. Wireless is worth it once the room is big enough that cables become a trip hazard, and then only a UHF system — the 2.4 GHz kind shares the airwaves with your Wi-Fi.
guide.gear.faq7.q: Can I use my soundbar or a small Bluetooth speaker for the vocals?
guide.gear.faq7.a: For the music, yes. For the microphone, no — soundbars and pocket Bluetooth speakers were never built for the sharp peaks a voice produces, so they distort at party volume and can be damaged. A party speaker with a mic input or a powered PA speaker is designed for exactly that, and it's the one thing in this guide worth spending on.
guide.gear.closing: Total damage for a setup that handles birthdays, holidays, and random Tuesday nights: one speaker, two mics, and a couple of cables. The song library, the queue, and the lyrics screen stay free forever — that part's on us.
guide.channels.title: The 6 Best YouTube Karaoke Channels for Free Karaoke | KaraoQ
guide.channels.metaDesc: The YouTube karaoke channels actually worth knowing — Sing King, KaraFun, Stingray, Party Tyme, Sing2Piano, and CC Karaoke — and how to turn them into a real karaoke night with a shared queue.
guide.channels.intro: YouTube quietly became the biggest karaoke library on earth — but the quality lives on a handful of dedicated channels that professionally produce backing tracks with on-screen lyrics. These six cover almost any song a party can throw at you. Search inside KaraoQ and their tracks show up automatically; queue them from everyone's phones and the night runs itself.
guide.channels.itemsIntro: Ordered roughly by how often they'll save your party. Between them: pop, rock, country, showtunes, and every wedding-reception staple ever written.
guide.channels.item1.name: Sing King
guide.channels.item1.body: The heavyweight — the biggest dedicated karaoke channel on YouTube, with thousands of polished tracks and new hits added fast. If a song was ever on the radio, Sing King probably has it, with clean instrumentals and crisp lyric timing.
guide.channels.item2.name: KaraFun
guide.channels.item2.body: The YouTube arm of the KaraFun karaoke company, so the production quality is studio-grade: faithful re-recordings, backing vocals where the original needs them, and reliable lyric sync across a huge catalog.
guide.channels.item3.name: Stingray Karaoke
guide.channels.item3.body: Formerly The Karaoke Channel — one of the oldest licensed karaoke libraries anywhere, now under the Stingray banner. Deep coverage of classics, country, and standards that younger channels skip, with proper scrolling lyrics.
guide.channels.item4.name: Party Tyme Karaoke
guide.channels.item4.body: Radio-quality backing tracks from Sybersound, a name karaoke bars have trusted for decades. Especially strong on decades hits and crowd-pleasers — the songs the whole room sings along to.
guide.channels.item5.name: Sing2Piano
guide.channels.item5.body: Piano-only backing tracks, and secretly the best channel for nervous singers — a solo piano is far more forgiving than a full arrangement. Also the go-to for stripped-back versions of big ballads.
guide.channels.item6.name: CC Karaoke
guide.channels.item6.body: A smaller creator-run channel with a devoted following, focused on doing karaoke properly: accurate lyrics, sensible keys, and current songs that the big channels haven't covered yet.
guide.channels.faq1.a: Yes. These channels publish their tracks free on YouTube, and KaraoQ plays them straight from YouTube at no cost — free to host, free to join, no subscription. You'll see the occasional ad, same as YouTube anywhere.
guide.channels.faq2.q: How do I run a party off these channels?
guide.channels.faq2.a: Create a KaraoQ room and share the QR code. Everyone searches from their own phone — results pull in tracks from all of these channels — and adds songs to one shared queue that plays back to back on your TV. No more passing a laptop around.
guide.channels.faq3.q: What if a song isn't on any karaoke channel?
guide.channels.faq3.a: Search the song name plus "karaoke" or "instrumental" — smaller channels cover an astonishing long tail. Failing that, a lyric video of the original works surprisingly well for songs everyone half-knows anyway.
guide.channels.faq4.q: Can I play these channels on my TV?
guide.channels.faq4.a: Yes — cast KaraoQ to the TV with AirPlay or Google Cast, plug in over HDMI, or use a streaming stick. The lyrics play full-screen while the queue keeps running from everyone's phones.
guide.channels.closing: Subscribe to a couple of these and your karaoke library updates itself forever — no discs, no downloads, no fees. Then let KaraoQ do the rest: one shared queue, everyone picking from their own phone, lyrics on the big screen.
